visual_features.distinctive_marks: black markings on the wings and tail, orange bill

description: The milky stork (Mycteria cinerea) is a medium-sized stork species inhabiting predominantly mangroves in Southeast Asia. It is native to Cambodia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Indonesia. Since the 1980s, the global population has declined from an estimated 5,000 to approximately 1,500 mature individuals due to habitat destruction, overfishing and illegal smuggling of chicks. It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List and on CITES Appendix I. The species is closely related to the painted stork (Mycteria leucocephala) and shares a clade with other members of the genus Mycteria. It is usually silent during non-breeding but utters a falsetto 'fizz' call during courtship displays at nests.
population_estimate: Approximately 1,500 mature individuals globally. The largest remaining population is on Sumatra, Indonesia (about 1,600 birds estimated in 2008-2009), with fewer than 500 in West Java. Very small populations persist in Cambodia (about 17 pairs in 2010) and Peninsular Malaysia (fewer than 10 birds in 2005). The population has declined by approximately 70% in South Sumatra between 1986 and 2008. The species is now very likely extinct in Thailand where it was historically recorded.
habitat: Predominantly a lowland coastal species inhabiting mangroves, tidal mudflats, shallow saline or freshwater pools, freshwater marshes, fishponds, rice paddies, and backswamps along river floodplains up to 15 km from the coast. Breeding requires extensive and undisturbed mangrove or riverine forest with tall trees (6-12 m) for nesting, and shallow pools within forests for juveniles to forage. In Cambodia, the species also disperses to the Tonle Sap Lake area during the wet season.
threats: Habitat destruction - mangrove clearing for aquaculture, agriculture and coastal development
Illegal wildlife trade - smuggling of chicks and eggs from nests
Overfishing reducing prey availability in foraging grounds
Nest disturbance and egg collection by local communities
Hybridization with painted storks in captivity and possibly in the wild
ecosystem_role: As a wading bird predator, the milky stork helps regulate fish and invertebrate populations in coastal wetland ecosystems. It serves as an indicator species for healthy mangrove and estuarine habitats. Its foraging activities in tidal mudflats and wetlands help cycle nutrients. The species' nesting colonies create nutrient-rich guano deposits that fertilize surrounding vegetation.
human_connection: The milky stork has cultural significance in parts of Indonesia and Malaysia as a distinctive coastal bird. Its dramatic population decline from an estimated 5,000 birds in the 1980s to about 1,500 today directly reflects the impact of mangrove destruction for shrimp farming and coastal development. Conservation efforts in Malaysia include captive breeding programs at the National Zoo of Malaysia and Singapore Zoo. Birdwatching tourism involving milky storks provides economic incentives for habitat protection in parts of Sumatra and Java.
what_students_can_do: Learn about the connection between mangrove forests and bird species like the milky stork
Support organizations working to protect Southeast Asian coastal wetlands
Reduce consumption of shrimp from unsustainable aquaculture that destroys mangrove habitats
Participate in coastal clean-up activities to reduce pollution in wetland ecosystems
Share information about endangered bird species with friends and family to raise awareness
fun_fact: The milky stork gets its name from the creamy yellow 'milky' tinge its white feathers develop during the breeding season.
These storks have specially adapted long, thick toes that prevent them from sinking into soft mud while foraging on tidal flats.
Milky storks are known to hybridize with closely related painted storks in captivity, producing offspring with a mix of features from both species.
